title: Negative: 2D bonded-lipid bilayers (lipid-2d) stay open ribbons and do not close into vesicles at 7 settings up to t=6000, including half density and recruitment-grown ribbons
summary: Follow-up to the lipid-2d sighting. Seven runs from a uniform random lipid gas (temperature, tail-attraction range, density 0.5-1.75x, and the membrane chemistry starting from 5-30% active lipid) were scored for solvent regions enclosed by lipid (holes.py). Every non-jammed run ends as open bilayer ribbons or branched ribbon networks with 0-1 enclosures of 14-18 sigma^2 (a few lipids' worth of solvent), never a vesicle; the dense run's 14 enclosures are gaps in a jammed packing. Recruitment from sparse nuclei grows ribbons to hundreds of lipids (5% -> 83% active) but they branch and join each other rather than close. Likely cause: in 2D a bilayer's open edge is two end caps whose cost does not grow with length, so nothing drives closure; vesicles in a particle membrane model probably need 3D, a much stronger end-cap penalty, or a driven asymmetry between leaflets.

finding.operator: 2D Cooke-Kremer-Deserno bonded amphiphiles (tail cos^2 attraction, implicit solvent), with and without autocatalytic precursor conversion
finding.control: 7 parameter points from the same random-gas start (runs.txt); enclosure count by holes.py
finding.result: 0-1 enclosed solvent regions of 14-18 sigma^2 per run in the 6 non-jammed runs at t=1800-6000; no closed vesicle; bilayer ribbons and branched networks only
